issue.title: CLAUDE.md hook-format: confirm tool_response, flag permissionDecisionReason + PermissionRequest field names as unvalidated, add async/rewake coverage
issue.context:
Found 2026-07-16 by the claude-code contract study (anthropics/claude-code public repo — CONTRACT docs/examples/plugins/changelog, NOT the closed engine). Every CLAUDE.md 'Claude Code Hook Response Format' claim cross-checked against Anthropic's own material.

CONFIRMED by Anthropic's SHIPPED security-guidance production hook (authoritative over teaching docs):
- PostToolUse field is tool_response (NOT tool_result): security_reminder_hook.py:913/925-933 reads tool_response.{stdout,stderr,interrupted}, with comment 'Bash tool_response has no exit_code field'. Wisphive's probe-verified value is CORRECT. IMPORTANT: Anthropic's own PUBLIC teaching docs mislabel it tool_result (SKILL.md:316, test-hook.sh:55, references/advanced.md:248) — so 'verify against the docs' hits a FALSE contradiction; the shipped security hook is the real source. Worth a one-line note in CLAUDE.md so a future session doesn't 'correct' tool_response back to tool_result.
- hookSpecificOutput{hookEventName}, permissionDecision allow|deny|ask, updatedInput, additionalContext: all CONFIRMED (security_reminder_hook.py:2175-2186; SKILL.md:145-152; CHANGELOG.md:2096/2422/1989).
- PostToolUse deny via exit 2 + stderr: CONFIRMED (bash_command_validator_example.py:78-79).
- hooks.json shape event->[{matcher,hooks:[{type,command|prompt,timeout?}]}], type in {command,prompt}: CONFIRMED (validate-hook-schema.sh:71-101).

UNSUPPORTED (not found anywhere in the contract material — NOT proven wrong, but reverse-engineered and unvalidated; matches Wisphive's own 'never guess hook fields' note):
- permissionDecisionReason: ZERO hits repo-wide. Plausibly engine-real but no contract file names it.
- PermissionRequest response field names decision.behavior and updatedPermissions: ZERO hits. The CAPABILITIES are changelog-confirmed (PermissionRequest can approve/deny, process 'always allow' suggestions, apply setMode, return updatedInput — CHANGELOG.md:4054/4005/1989) but the literal field names are unconfirmed.
=> These two should be RE-PROBED against a live Claude Code (the docs/research/hook-probe/ pattern) before Wisphive relies on the exact field names; until then CLAUDE.md should mark them reverse-engineered.

EVENT LIST: contract blesses a core of 9 (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart, SessionEnd, PreCompact, Notification — validate-hook-schema.sh:41 VALID_EVENTS) + PermissionRequest (changelog). The rest of CLAUDE.md's HookEventType (PostToolUseFailure, Elicitation, ElicitationResult, InstructionsLoaded, SubagentStart, StopFailure, ConfigChange, TeammateIdle, TaskCompleted, WorktreeCreate, WorktreeRemove, PostCompact) are UNSUPPORTED here — but the validator is a plugin-authoring aid, not the engine registry, so absence is NOT evidence they're unreal. Leave them; just don't cite this study as confirming them.

COVERAGE GAP (not an error): Anthropic's security-guidance hooks.json uses keys CLAUDE.md doesn't mention — 'if' (command matcher like 'Bash(git commit:*)'), asyncRewake/rewakeMessage/rewakeSummary, and response keys async/asyncTimeout/metrics (security-guidance/hooks/hooks.json:40-51, ensure_agent_sdk.py:195/225, security_reminder_hook.py:193-226). Real Anthropic capabilities Wisphive could use for async/rewake hook behavior; note if/when relevant.
issue.acceptance:
1. CLAUDE.md notes tool_response is confirmed by Anthropic's shipped security hook AND that Anthropic's public plugin-dev docs mislabel it tool_result — so the shipped hook, not the docs, is the source of truth.
2. CLAUDE.md marks permissionDecisionReason and the PermissionRequest response field names (decision.behavior, updatedPermissions) as reverse-engineered / unvalidated, pending a live re-probe.
3. A live re-probe of those specific fields is filed or done (docs/research/hook-probe/ pattern) before any code depends on the exact field names.
4. Edits scoped to CLAUDE.md's hook section only; no behavior change. Stage only CLAUDE.md (concurrent sessions in tree).

issue.title: ADR: anchor the Wisphive gate ABOVE the agent's write reach — cross-provider gate-anchoring + the USE-1/USE-2 app-server distinction
issue.context:
Synthesis of the 2026-07-16 authoritative-source study (openai/codex @315195492c real Rust + anthropics/claude-code contract material). Two independent findings converge on one principle that should be an ADR, because it is the security foundation for the Chat surface and it constrains all future managed-spawn work.

=== PRINCIPLE: anchor the gate above the agent's same-UID write reach ===
Wisphive's gate today is fenced, not anchored: managed Claude spawns pass --dangerously-skip-permissions + --setting-sources project (the hook is the only gate, and the agent — same UID — can write ~/.claude/settings.json); managed Codex spawns pass --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust (suppresses trust for ALL enabled hooks, itr#471). Both fence the risk. The source study found BOTH providers offer a way to ANCHOR the gate above the agent's reach instead:

CLAUDE (contract-confirmed, engine-enforcement closed): a MANAGED settings tier in a root-owned system dir (examples/mdm/README.md:15-24) 'sits at the top of precedence and cannot be overridden by users', exposing allowManagedHooksOnly (block all user/project hooks), allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly, and disableBypassPermissionsMode:'disable' (kills --dangerously-skip-permissions, honored even against a hook's own setMode:bypassPermissions, CHANGELOG.md:1989). Placing wisphive-hook as a MANAGED hook + allowManagedHooksOnly anchors it beyond a same-UID agent's edit. CAVEAT: whether a managed PreToolUse hook is a HARD gate vs advisory is closed engine behavior — take on Anthropic's documented word, verify by probe.

CODEX (source-confirmed): requirements.toml / MDM 'requirements' clamp (config_requirements.rs:1302-1398) applied AFTER request+CLI merge and WINS; allow_managed_hooks_only strips all non-managed hooks at discovery INDEPENDENT of bypass_hook_trust (discovery.rs:57-82); client cannot disable (ignore_managed_requirements is internal test-only, state.rs:40-46). PLUS the per-hook trust-registration path (itr#570): write our hook's trusted_hash, spawn WITHOUT bypass, Codex's own trust gate refuses foreign hooks.

SHARED CAVEAT (both): these floors are OPERATOR-PROVISIONED and OFF BY DEFAULT, and neither covers every vector (Codex: not the arbitrary config-key nor the exec/fs/config-write sibling methods; Claude: enforcement unseen). So they are DEFENSE-IN-DEPTH that strengthens the gate, NOT a replacement for it. The ADR must say this plainly so a future reader does not treat 'managed tier' as a complete solution.

=== THE USE-1 / USE-2 APP-SERVER DISTINCTION (the other half of the ADR) ===
The #566 source verdict established that 'can Wisphive speak Codex app-server safely' has TWO answers:
USE 1 — Wisphive-internal control plane: short-lived, Wisphive-authored process, every message written by Wisphive, agent never on the pipe (hooks/list probe #569; trusted_hash write #570). SAFE — no steering because no other client.
USE 2 — agent session transport (Chat over app-server): agent turns flow over the pipe; config/steering/sibling-methods become agent-reachable. UNSAFE unless (i) closed typed constructor pins every steering field per start/resume/fork/turn, (ii) config map refused/allowlisted incl bypass_hook_trust, (iii) client->server METHOD allowlist blocks exec/fs/config-write/shellCommand. Verdict: do NOT ship app-server as an agent transport in Chat v1.

This distinction is non-obvious, had real alternatives (we nearly treated app-server as one thing), is security-critical, and future work will ask 'why can #569/#570 use app-server but Chat can't' — the exact test for an ADR per CLAUDE.md.
issue.acceptance:
1. ADR filed under docs/decisions/ (next number) capturing: the anchor-above-reach principle; the two provider mechanisms with file:line; the shared 'defense-in-depth not replacement, off by default' caveat; and the USE-1/USE-2 app-server distinction with the three-part USE-2 audit requirement.
2. It records what is SOURCE-CONFIRMED (Codex requirements clamp; Codex trust model) vs CONTRACT-ASSERTED-ENGINE-CLOSED (Claude managed-hook hard-enforcement) — the reader must know which claims are verified and which rest on vendor docs pending a probe.
3. Cross-links itr#566 (USE-2 verdict), #569 (USE-1 probe), #570 (USE-1 trust-write, Codex anchor), #564 (stream-json Chat transport), #471 (the bypass this supersedes), and ADR-0009 (the amendment #569 already requires).
4. Status Proposed; it does not flip until a Chat design commits to a gate-anchoring mechanism and a probe confirms the Claude managed-hook enforcement.

issue.title: EPIC: herdr-inspired UX — attention-routing, notifications & navigation
issue.context:
Adopt the highest-value UX patterns surfaced by the read-only herdr survey (docs/research/herdr-ux-mining.md), adapted to wisphive's gating-first identity.

## Framing
herdr is a terminal multiplexer that *runs* agents; wisphive is a human-in-the-loop control plane that *gates* their tool calls. herdr's real value is attention-routing UX — which maps almost perfectly onto wisphive's core job (route a human to the agent that needs a decision). herdr's *steering* affordances (agents spawning/driving panes) are explicitly OUT OF SCOPE — they would bypass the gate.

## Guardrails (apply to every child)
- Navigation/notification/status surfaces stay **read-only**: they may select/reveal/alert, never resolve a decision. Only the TUI/web/permission surface resolves.
- Notifications remain informational (never carry an approve action); redaction (protocol::redact, itr#89) runs over any tool_input shown.
- Attention ordering for a gating tool: pending-human-decision > timing-out-soon > done-unseen > working > idle.
- No agent-facing write/steering verbs; no unsandboxed plugin ABI; no screen-scraping status detection.

## Source
Full survey, ranked table, deep-dives, and security appendix: docs/research/herdr-ux-mining.md

issue.title: EPIC: Session survival across daemon restart — respawn now, live FD-handoff next (herdr model)
issue.context:
Make important terminal + agent sessions survive a wisphive daemon restart, adopting herdr's model. Research + costed plans: docs/research/terminal-session-survival.md.

## Reframe (two axes)
Detach/reattach across a *client* disconnect already works (daemon owns the PTY; clients subscribe to a broadcast channel). The gap is surviving the *daemon process* going away. Split on: {live process must survive | session just comes back} x {planned restart | crash}. Honest ceiling: NO system (incl. herdr) keeps a live process alive across an ungraceful crash — herdr's live survival is an opt-in graceful FD-handoff for planned upgrades only.

## Root cause today
The daemon IS the PTY owner. PTY children are parented to the daemon (no setsid/process_group), teardown kills them (shutdown_all, terminal.rs:459-469), startup marks survivors orphaned (terminals.rs:278-288), live handles are in-memory (env_json even bound NULL), and managed agents have NO persistence table at all.

## Three plans (PO decisions recorded)
- **Plan A — respawn/reconcile ("sessions come back"): BUILD NOW.** Pin important sessions, persist full respawn spec, startup-reconcile (respawn in cwd + seed scrollback from terminal_events), managed-agent persistence, agent-pane resume via #582. Respawned child re-enters the hook gate cleanly. Caveat: mid-flight process restarts.
- **Plan B — live process survives a PLANNED restart (SCM_RIGHTS FD-handoff): EXPLORE (the target).** herdr's --handoff mechanism. PO: the brief gate-transfer gap during a planned upgrade is minor (terminal-native prompt backs it up) AND MUST BE SURFACED to the user. Spike precursor = #581.
- **Plan C — VIP (Very Important Processes): LAST, but evaluate first.** Separate PTY host outside the daemon so sessions survive even a crash and can observe wisphive's own upgrade remotely. A PTY host could subsume Plan B — the C-spike decides build order.

## Cross-links
Related epic #573 (herdr-inspired UX) children: #580 (restart-survival matrix docs/ui), #581 (hot-swap spike = Plan B precursor), #582 (provider-native resume registry = Plan A agent-resume piece).

issue.title: spike(arch): VIP PTY-host — survive crash + observe wisphive's own upgrade; does it subsume Plan B?
issue.context:

issue.title: feat(gate): authorize the upgrade/handoff action itself (password/passkey) — you can't lower the gate un-authorized
issue.context:
A handoff upgrade (Plan B, #595-#597) opens a brief enforcement gap while the gate transfers between daemons (#596). Therefore INITIATING that upgrade is itself a privileged control-plane action and must be authorized — you cannot let an unauthenticated caller, or (critically) a GATED AGENT, trigger the one operation that momentarily lowers the gate.

## What
Gate the upgrade/handoff action behind explicit operator authorization, reusing wisphive's own auth model rather than inventing one:
- Web: require a fresh Argon2id password re-auth or a WebAuthn passkey assertion (auth.rs) — a sudo-style step-up, not just a valid device bearer — before an upgrade/handoff can be initiated. Mirrors the 'sudo-gated to mint' pattern from the enterprise enroll flow (#313).
- CLI/local: require an explicit operator confirmation/authorization step for the handoff upgrade path; an agent-driven invocation is refused.
- A gated agent must NEVER be able to initiate a gate-transferring upgrade. This extends the control-plane self-protection posture (allow_self_modification=false / itr#425): triggering an upgrade is a self-modification of the gate and routes to human authorization, never auto-approve.

## Why
The whole point of #596 is that the brief gate gap is acceptable BECAUSE it's operator-initiated and surfaced. That argument only holds if the action is genuinely operator-gated. Without this, the disclosed gap becomes an exploitable bypass: 'trigger an upgrade to slip a call through the transfer window.'

## Audit
The authorized upgrade is recorded to the decision/audit trail (who authorized, when, from which device) so the gate-transfer window is attributable.

Reconciles with ADR-0010 (voluntary authenticated transfer vs involuntary integrity failure) and ADR-0001 (the fallback posture inside the window).

issue.title: stop split: emergency SIGKILL-now vs graceful TERM-grace-KILL ladder
issue.context: From mission no-silent-failures 603/L5 (#561). The repo's own recon (docs/research/t3code-recon.md §L6 c4) argues the TERM→grace→KILL ladder is wrong as the ONLY operator stop: the 2s grace is a setsid-escape window invisible to group-scoped ESRCH confirmation, and under default auto_approve_level=all the grace means 'keep running unsupervised for 2s'. #561 implemented the frozen DoD (ladder) and documented the residual in the STOP_TERM_GRACE rationale + plan-loop-supervisor rail 7. Decide + build the second control: an emergency stop (SIGKILL-to-group immediately, no grace) exposed as e.g. wisphive agent stop --force / TUI hard-stop, with the ladder remaining the default. Also weigh the CLI SOCKET_TIMEOUT=5s coupling (agent.rs:13) — any longer grace design times out client-side before the daemon's verdict (silent-ish failure).
issue.acceptance: Operator can invoke an immediate group-SIGKILL stop with confirmed-gone semantics; default stop keeps the documented ladder; CLI does not time out before the daemon verdict on either path.

notes.content: Scope addition from 603/L5 review (B-A10 registration): the emergency-stop design should also (a) give stop outcomes an audit trail — today stop verdicts are reply-only (AgentStopResponse/Error), shutdown_all ladder failures are warn!-only with no client and no persisted record, nothing is queryable post-hoc via wisphive audit; (b) route web-origin StopAgent failures through the typed CommandError+correlation_id channel (itr#567 covered spawn refusals only); (c) reuse the shutdown_all JoinSet pattern for wave aggregation — N serial inline ladders = N×4s worst case on one connection.

issue.context:

issue.title: Terminal replay denied for the operator's own web device: TUI/CLI-created sessions can never restore scrollback in the web UI (replay ACL has no grant path)
issue.context:
Found during the 2026-07-05 smoke item 'Terminal touch-to-scroll on a real phone/tablet' (docs/smoke/CHECKLIST.md, itr#445). Touch-to-scroll ITSELF works — verified: scrollback generated while attached scrolls correctly by touch. The reported 'touch scroll doesn't work on mobile' is a downstream symptom of this.

Browser console on re-attach:
  Terminal error: terminal replay denied: requester is not the session creator or in the replay ACL

Mechanism (crates/wisphive_daemon/src/server.rs):
- requester identity is 'human:web:<device_id>' for web clients, 'human:tui' for TUI/CLI (server.rs:1210-1212)
- evaluate_replay_access(): authored = (created_by == requester); explicit_access = replay_acl.contains(requester) (server.rs:1246-1258)
- allowed() = session_known && (authored || explicit_access) (server.rs:1225-1227)
- replay_acl defaults to EMPTY (terminal.rs:216, terminal.rs:1397); denial emitted at server.rs:3515-3531

Effect: a terminal created via 'wisphive term new' / TUI is authored 'human:tui'. The operator's OWN authenticated web device requests as 'human:web:<id>', never matches, ACL is empty, and there is NO affordance anywhere to add a device to replay_acl. So switching away from and back to such a session in the web UI restores only the current screen — scrollback is permanently unrecoverable from the browser, on desktop and mobile alike. Ruled out as causes: itr#284 'nothing generated yet' (scrollback WAS generated while attached), zero-height viewport (live DOM: .xterm-viewport clientHeight=930), touch-action/CSS (pinch-zoom works), event plumbing (same-page touch scroll works).

Note the security intent is sound — one device should not replay another's terminal. The defect is that the operator's own cross-surface access is collateral, with no grant path and a raw error string as the only feedback.
issue.acceptance: The operator can restore scrollback in the web UI for a terminal they created from the CLI/TUI. Either (a) sessions created by the same authenticated human resolve to a common identity so 'authored' matches across TUI/CLI/web surfaces, or (b) there is an explicit, auditable affordance to grant a device replay access (populating replay_acl), or (c) both. A denial must surface as actionable UI guidance naming the grant path — not a raw 'replay denied' console error. Cross-device replay by an unauthorized device remains denied and audited.

notes.content:
PO SMOKE-TEST EVIDENCE 2026-07-19 — 4-cell cross-device matrix, captured on a rebuilt+restarted daemon carrying the itr#624 seeded-attach change (uncommitted working tree). Each cell: create a terminal on one surface, run 'seq -w 1 300', then try to scroll from each surface.

| created on | viewed on WEB            | viewed on DEVICE (phone)    |
| web        | FULL scrollback, works   | PARTIAL - only back to 230  |
| device     | DENIED - screen-only,    | FULL, scrolls to session    |
|            | 'terminal replay denied',| start                       |
|            | shows only 261-299       |                             |

CONFIRMS: created_by is a PER-DEVICE identity (human:web:<device_id>), so the operator's OWN two browsers are strangers to each other. The creator device gets history; every other device is ACL-denied and falls back to screen-only.

WHY THIS IS NOW URGENT (it was latent before): the itr#624 seeded-attach change turns a SYMMETRIC limitation (nobody got scrollback on re-attach) into an ASYMMETRIC one (creator device does, others don't). The PO initially experienced this as 'the scroll wheel is broken on web' — i.e. the boundary reads as a broken feature, not as a permission decision. Shipping seeded attach without #623's grant path means every multi-surface operator will hit this and misread it as a bug.

OPEN QUESTION worth investigating: in the web-created / device-viewed cell the phone reached line 230 rather than getting screen-only. If the phone was attached live while 'seq' ran, that history is legitimately live-forwarded output and is fine. But if a NON-CREATOR device received ~70 lines of catchup history it was not authorized for, that is an ACL boundary inconsistency and should be treated as a security finding. Determine which before closing.

Also note the denial IS surfaced as a raw 'terminal replay denied' string rather than actionable UI — #623's acceptance already requires guidance naming the grant path.

PO DIRECTION 2026-07-19 — identity should be PER-USER, not per-device.

The PO's call: 'We need to be able to cross the ACL boundary - it should be per user not per device if possible.' That selects option (a) from this issue's acceptance criteria (common identity across surfaces) over option (b) (a per-device grant affordance), though a grant path may still be wanted for genuinely foreign devices.

Also resolved: the 230-line anomaly in the web-created/device-viewed cell is BENIGN, not an ACL leak. The PO confirms the phone tab was already open and attached while 'seq -w 1 300' ran, so that history was live-forwarded output the device legitimately received. No unauthorized catchup occurred.

DESIGN NOTE for whoever implements this — the trust-boundary reasoning should be recorded, ideally as an ADR:
- Today 'created_by' is 'human:web:<device_id>' or 'human:tui'. Every web device belongs to the SAME single operator (there is one web password; devices are just separately-issued bearer tokens). So the current per-device split gives little real security benefit against an attacker holding a valid device token — such an attacker is already the operator, and per CLAUDE.md a web-token XSS is device compromise anyway. What per-device identity mostly achieves today is locking the legitimate operator out of their own history across their own surfaces.
- Counter-argument to weigh honestly: a REVOKED or compromised device arguably should not be able to pull history from sessions it never created. A per-user identity widens what a stolen token reaches. Mitigation: bind replay authorization to the live device-revocation check rather than to session authorship, so revoking a device immediately cuts its history access.
- Practical shape: resolve TUI/CLI ('human:tui') and all web devices of the operator to one principal (e.g. 'human:operator'), keep 'replay_acl' for genuinely foreign principals, and keep the denial path audited.
- UX requirement stands regardless: a denial must surface as actionable UI naming the grant path, not the raw 'terminal replay denied' string. The PO first experienced this boundary as 'the scroll wheel is broken on web'.

URGENCY RAISED: the itr#624 attach-seed change (committed) makes this boundary user-visible — creator device gets scrollback, every other surface silently does not.

ADR-0013 filed (commit b314d0d): docs/decisions/0013-per-user-replay-identity-bound-to-device-revocation.md — Status Accepted, records the DECISION only; this issue remains the implementation.

Decided: replay authorization becomes PER-USER (TUI/CLI + all operator web devices resolve to one principal), and authorization binds to the LIVE device-revocation check at request time rather than to session authorship.

Key implementation constraints the ADR imposes on this issue:
- Do NOT re-key authorization on 'created_by'; it returns to being provenance metadata only.
- The revocation check must be evaluated LIVE PER REQUEST. Never cache it for the lifetime of a connection — a revoked device would retain history access until it reconnected. Treat this as a correctness constraint on any future caching.
- Retain replay_acl for genuinely FOREIGN principals; explicit grant is still the right semantic there.
- Denials must surface as actionable UI naming the remedy, not the raw 'terminal replay denied' string.
- Any new history-bearing surface (mobile pairing, remote access) inherits this model and the same live check.

Accepted costs recorded in the ADR: a compromised not-yet-revoked device now reaches the operator's history rather than only sessions it created; revocation becomes a load-bearing security control on the hot path; per-device compartmentalization is gone so revocation is the only lever; and multi-operator support becomes an explicit future decision requiring the ADR to be revisited rather than quietly extended.

ADR-0013 AMENDMENT 1 (commit 8fca9f7) — step-up re-authentication is now part of this issue's required design, not optional.

PO direction: a remote device must have authenticated within a recent window (default 2-3h, configurable) to view or request a session it is NOT already attached to. Inside the window, and for sessions the device is already in, access stays frictionless.

Why it matters for implementation: revocation (the main ADR-0013 control) is REACTIVE — it protects only after the operator notices a compromise and acts. Step-up is the PROACTIVE half: an attacker with an exfiltrated token but no password/passkey cannot cross into unfamiliar history at all. Implement BOTH; neither subsumes the other.

Implementation requirements added by the amendment:
- Add last_authenticated_at per web device; the recency predicate joins the live revocation check on the replay/attach authorization path. BOTH are per-request state — same no-caching constraint.
- Session authorship is DEMOTED to a step-up TRIGGER, not an authorization boundary. created_by + current attachment answer 'does this need a challenge?' only. Permission remains per-user + live revocation.
- Scope to REMOTE surfaces only. TUI/CLI runs as the operator's UID and is trusted per ADR-0008 — no auth session to step up; applying it there is theater.
- A failed/abandoned step-up must AUDIT and NOTIFY, not just deny. A party holding a valid token who cannot authenticate is a high-signal compromise indicator; this is the cheapest detection point in the system.
- Step-up failure, unavailability, or an unreadable auth timestamp FAILS CLOSED per ADR-0010.
- The recency timestamp must be SERVER-SIDE state. Never client-supplied or client-adjustable — a clock the attacker controls is not a boundary.
- Passkey/biometric should be the default challenge path; this boundary is crossed most on mobile, where a typed password is punishing.

Known limit recorded in the ADR: this does NOT defend against a live XSS in the operator's own browser, which shares the origin and can ride a legitimate re-auth. Its strength is against an exfiltrated token replayed out-of-band. Do not let it justify relaxing XSS discipline.

SEE itr#625 — device-token accumulation materially amplifies this issue. Every web login mints a NEW device_id via a plain INSERT (no upsert, no stable per-browser identity), and tokens never expire. The operator's real install carries 6 ACTIVE device rows for 2 physical devices.

Consequence for this issue's design: because a re-login produces a new device_id, the SAME physical device becomes a stranger to ITSELF and loses replay access to sessions it created. That is a second, independent path to the 'my own device can't see my scrollback' symptom — distinct from the cross-device case in the smoke matrix, and it would persist even for a single-device operator.

It also undermines ADR-0013's core control: that ADR makes LIVE DEVICE REVOCATION the load-bearing security boundary replacing session authorship. Revocation cannot be load-bearing if device records proliferate uncontrollably and the operator cannot tell which row corresponds to which browser (three rows here are all named 'Android (Chrome)'). Implementing ADR-0013 on top of the current minting behaviour would give a false sense of control.

RECOMMENDATION: treat itr#625 as a prerequisite for, or at minimum co-delivered with, this issue. Stable per-browser device identity is what makes both 'per-user principal' and 'revocation as the firebreak' coherent.

Known limit recorded in the ADR: this does NOT defend against a live XSS in the operator's own browser, which shares the origin and can ride a legitimate re-auth. Its strength is against an exfiltrated token replayed out-of-band. Do not let it justify relaxing XSS discipline.

SEE itr#625 — device-token accumulation materially amplifies this issue. Every web login mints a NEW device_id via a plain INSERT (no upsert, no stable per-browser identity), and tokens never expire. The operator's real install carries 6 ACTIVE device rows for 2 physical devices.

Consequence for this issue's design: because a re-login produces a new device_id, the SAME physical device becomes a stranger to ITSELF and loses replay access to sessions it created. That is a second, independent path to the 'my own device can't see my scrollback' symptom — distinct from the cross-device case in the smoke matrix, and it would persist even for a single-device operator.

It also undermines ADR-0013's core control: that ADR makes LIVE DEVICE REVOCATION the load-bearing security boundary replacing session authorship. Revocation cannot be load-bearing if device records proliferate uncontrollably and the operator cannot tell which row corresponds to which browser (three rows here are all named 'Android (Chrome)'). Implementing ADR-0013 on top of the current minting behaviour would give a false sense of control.

RECOMMENDATION: treat itr#625 as a prerequisite for, or at minimum co-delivered with, this issue. Stable per-browser device identity is what makes both 'per-user principal' and 'revocation as the firebreak' coherent.

issue.title: Terminal scrollback unreachable after page load until a window resize — xterm scrollable area comes up mis-sized (affects BOTH wheel and touch; NOT a touch bug)
issue.context:
Found during the 2026-07-05 smoke item 'Terminal touch-to-scroll on a real phone/tablet' (docs/smoke/CHECKLIST.md, itr#445). Supersedes the earlier impression that touch scroll worked.

OBSERVED (real device, Android/Chrome, in-scope per itr#283; also reproduces in Chrome DevTools mobile emulation): a vertical touch-drag inside the terminal makes content move, but it is the SAME ROWS SLIDING AROUND — no earlier scrollback text is ever revealed. The xterm buffer viewport is not paging. Wheel/trackpad scroll on desktop DOES page real scrollback, so xterm's own buffer scrolling is healthy; only the touch path fails. Intermittently the gesture instead scrolls an ancestor pane ('pane jacking').

SUSPECTED MECHANISM (needs confirmation, do not treat as established):
1. In TerminalView.tsx onTouchMove, preventDefault()/stopPropagation() are only reached AFTER the drag has travelled a full row (offsetRows !== appliedOffset). Every touchmove before that returns with the event neither prevented nor stopped, leaving the opening frames of the gesture available to xterm 6's own .xterm-scrollable-element and to the overflow ancestor (<main class="content"> is scrollable). That window is deliberate (itr#480, preserve near-tap focus) but may be what lets native scrolling claim the drag.
2. Possible that term.scrollToLine() does not move the rendered viewport in xterm 6, which uses a VS Code-style .xterm-scrollable-element. Live DOM confirms .xterm-viewport is an EMPTY vestigial div (clientHeight 930) while real content lives in its sibling .xterm-scrollable-element.

WHY THIS SHIPPED: TerminalView.test.tsx asserts the handler calls xterm's scroll API with the correct signed row delta — against a MOCK, under jsdom (no layout). It proves the arithmetic, never that the viewport moves. There is no committed test that exercises real touch against a real viewport (itr#479).

RULED OUT: itr#284/#623 no-scrollback-after-reattach (scrollback WAS generated on the same page without switching); zero-height viewport (clientHeight 930); touch-action/CSS blocking events (pinch-zoom works, single-finger reaches handler); iOS Safari scope exclusion (device is Android/Chrome).
issue.acceptance: A vertical touch-drag inside the terminal pages the xterm scrollback buffer so previously-unseen earlier output becomes visible, and dragging back returns to the live tail — verified on real hardware, not emulation. No native pane or ancestor scrolling occurs during the gesture (no pane jacking). Tap-to-focus, the on-screen keyboard, and the itr#480 near-tap behaviour still work. Backed by a committed regression test that asserts actual viewport/buffer movement (e.g. buffer.active.viewportY or rendered text changing), NOT merely that a scroll API was called on a mock.

notes.content:
ROOT CAUSE REFRAMED 2026-07-19 — this is NOT a touch bug. The touch handler is very likely innocent.

DECISIVE NEW EVIDENCE (product owner, real observation): immediately after a PAGE REFRESH, before any resize, WHEEL/trackpad scroll ALSO FAILS. Resizing the browser window restores scrolling for BOTH wheel and touch. So scrollback is unreachable by ANY input method until a resize occurs.

That demotes both original hypotheses (the preventDefault/stopPropagation gap, and scrollToLine being a no-op). The real defect is a terminal SIZING/INITIALIZATION RACE: xterm's custom scrollable area comes up mis-sized on mount, leaving nothing to page into until the ResizeObserver -> fit() recomputes it.

TerminalView.tsx:51-55 already predicts this in its own comment: 'Flex layout isn't guaranteed to be settled in the same tick as mount. Fit once synchronously so we have a best-effort size, then again in rAF so the viewport matches the final container height — otherwise the scrollable area can end up mis-sized until a window resize forces a recompute.' The syncFit() + single requestAnimationFrame(syncFit) mitigation at lines 66-67 is evidently insufficient.

Suspected why: web fonts not loaded when the rAF fit runs (wrong cell metrics -> wrong rows/cols), and/or flex layout settling more than one frame after mount.

This also explains the earlier confusion: the live console reading of .xterm-viewport clientHeight=930 looked healthy because the window had already been resized by then; and 'same rows sliding around' is what a mis-sized scroll area looks like when there is nothing to page into.

REVISED ACCEPTANCE: scrolling into scrollback works IMMEDIATELY after a page refresh with NO resize, via BOTH wheel and touch, proven by previously-unseen EARLIER TEXT becoming visible. Regression test must load fresh and scroll without any resize.

ROOT CAUSE CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-07-19 (supersedes the 'sizing race' note above — that framing was WRONG).

PROVEN root cause, instrumented in real Chromium against a real daemon + real PTY: the attach catchup carried ONLY the current vt100 screen (contents_formatted()), so after any page refresh / re-attach the client xterm buffer contained ZERO scrollback. Measured: baseY=0, length=54 (== rows) after refresh+attach, while xterm's own scroll dimensions were HEALTHY (cellHeight 15, canvas 810, scrollDims consistent). Wheel and touch both no-oped because there was nothing to page into. After new live output on the same page: baseY=303, and wheel+touch paged immediately WITHOUT any resize.

This is the ORIGINAL itr#284 framing (server-authoritative-scrollback-on-attach), not a sizing race and not a touch bug. The touch handler was never modified and pages correctly whenever data exists.

'Resizing the browser fixes it' was a RED HERRING: resize reflow manufactured exactly ONE line of scrollback (baseY 0->1). NOTE: this one-line measurement is not yet fully reconciled with the PO's lived report that resizing 'allows it to scroll the terminal output again', which sounded like more than one line. Treat as an open loose end.

Also disproven along the way: the preventDefault/stopPropagation ordering gap, term.scrollToLine() being a no-op, and zero-height viewport. Five wrong root causes preceded this one; the decisive evidence was buffer state (baseY/length), not code reading.

itr#623 remains UNTOUCHED and still real: a CLI/TUI-created session ('human:tui') attached from a web device still gets screen-only, so the operator still cannot get scrollback for their own CLI-created terminals.

issue.title: Every web login mints a NEW permanent device token; old tokens never expire — 6 live credentials for 2 physical devices
issue.context:
Found during 2026-07-19 smoke testing while investigating itr#623 (per-device replay identity).

OBSERVED on the operator's real install — 'wisphive web devices list' shows NINE device rows, SIX still active, for what the operator confirms should be TWO physical devices (one Mac, one Android phone):
  9ca507ac Mac (Chrome)      10.0.0.230  last seen 2026-07-19 08:33  active
  9b538d7f passkey-cd6feb88  127.0.0.1   last seen 2026-07-19 09:10  active
  4e46cec4 passkey-cd6feb88  127.0.0.1   last seen 2026-07-08        active
  59ffbd6a Android (Chrome)  10.0.0.176  last seen 2026-07-07        active
  575ef4fb Android (Chrome)  10.0.0.122  last seen 2026-07-05        active
  05c79ede Android (Chrome)  10.0.0.138  last seen 2026-07-19 09:14  active
  cd6feb88 Mac (Chrome)      127.0.0.1   last seen 2026-07-04        active

MECHANISM (crates/wisphive_daemon/src/state/web_auth.rs): insert_web_device() is a plain 'INSERT INTO web_devices (id, name, token_hash, created_at)' with a caller-supplied fresh UUIDv4. There is no upsert, no stable device identity, and no retirement of a prior record for the same browser. Passkey enrollment appears to mint yet another row ('passkey-<parent-device-id>'). last_seen_at IS tracked (line ~67, ~338) but nothing consumes it: grep finds NO expiry, NO TTL, and NO stale-device pruning anywhere in the module. Tokens are valid indefinitely until manually revoked.

WHY THIS IS A SECURITY ISSUE, not just clutter:
1. Unbounded accumulation of LIVE credentials. Each login leaves a permanently-valid bearer token behind. Tokens live in browser localStorage, so any old browser profile, disk backup, or synced profile still holds a working credential. The oldest active token here was last used 15 days ago and still authenticates.
2. No natural expiry means the blast radius of any past token exposure never shrinks on its own.
3. The operator has no way to tell which row is which browser — names collide ('Android (Chrome)' x3) and only the IP/last-seen distinguishes them, so safe manual cleanup is guesswork and risks revoking the session in active use.

WHY IT AMPLIFIES itr#623 / ADR-0013: replay authorization is currently keyed on a PER-DEVICE identity (human:web:<device_id>). Because a re-login mints a NEW device_id, the SAME physical device becomes a stranger to ITSELF after re-logging in, losing replay access to terminal sessions it created. This likely explains part of the inconsistent cross-device scrollback behaviour observed in itr#623's smoke matrix, beyond DHCP churn. ADR-0013 makes device revocation a load-bearing security control — that control is undermined if device records proliferate uncontrollably and the operator cannot confidently identify them.
issue.acceptance: A browser that logs in again reuses its existing device record rather than minting a new one, OR the previous record is explicitly retired so live credentials do not accumulate. Device tokens have a bounded lifetime (idle expiry and/or absolute TTL, configurable) enforced server-side, and expired devices are visibly distinguished from active ones in 'wisphive web devices list'. Passkey enrollment does not silently create an additional device row. Device rows carry enough distinguishing information (stable per-browser identity or operator-editable label) that the operator can safely revoke a specific device without guessing which row is the session they are currently using. Existing accumulated rows are addressable — a documented or tooled path to prune stale devices without a full reset-password wipe.

issue.title: Attach seed/live seam can DROP and DUPLICATE terminal output — ADR-0012's "never both" invariant is false
issue.context:
Found by an independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of commit e3d29b9, 2026-07-19.

The TermAttach arm captures next_seq at server.rs:3217, then performs MULTIPLE AWAITED DB operations, builds and writes the catchup, and only subscribes to the live broadcast at server.rs:3280. The window between those points is not atomic.

DROP: capture next_seq=N; frame N is parsed, assigned and broadcast while the attach is still querying/writing catchup; the SQL seed excludes it (seq < N) and no receiver existed when it was broadcast. If it arrived after catchup_snapshot(), it is absent from BOTH the seed and live delivery. With enough output, affected frames can also scroll out of the current screen and vanish from this attachment entirely.

DUPLICATE: the producer updates the parser BEFORE assigning a sequence and broadcasting (terminal.rs:783). If the reader is preempted between parsing and next_seq(), the attach can snapshot a parser that already includes that frame, then subscribe, then receive the same frame live once the reader assigns N (accepted because N >= next_seq).

CONSEQUENCE: ADR-0012 asserts an exclusive before_seq bound means the live forwarder 'can never re-deliver seeded frames'. That claim is FALSE as written. The exclusive SQL bound only separates persisted seed rows from live frames; it does not make the parser snapshot, the sequence boundary, and the subscription atomic. The ADR must be corrected as part of this fix.
issue.acceptance: Attaching to a terminal under continuous output delivers each frame exactly once — no gaps and no duplicates — with the seed, parser snapshot, and live subscription established atomically with respect to the sequence boundary (e.g. subscribe before snapshotting, then de-duplicate by seq; or hold the assignment lock across snapshot+subscribe). Covered by a test that attaches WHILE output is streaming and asserts the received byte stream is exactly the produced stream. ADR-0012 is amended so its stated invariant matches the implementation.
issue.close_reason: Fixed in dc63cad. Parser mutex = sequence-assignment lock; attach_with captures boundary+snapshot+subscription+high-water in one critical section; reader ingest fuses vt100 update + seq assignment; bounded persistence settle before the seed read. Deterministic red->green reproductions of both interleavings (gatr itr626-red: DROP=0 copies, DUP=2 copies; itr626-green: both exactly-once) plus mid-stream exactly-once acceptance test. Gates: itr626-daemon-tests 457+1+28 green, itr626-clippy green, itr626-e2e 24/24. ADR-0012 amended (Correction 1 resolution + true invariant in Decision).

notes.content: Fix implemented: parser mutex doubles as sequence-assignment lock; attach_with captures boundary+snapshot+subscription+high-water in one critical section; bounded persistence settle before seed read. Deterministic red/green repro: gatr tags itr626-red (DROP=0 copies, DUP=2 copies) and itr626-green. Full daemon suite 457+1+28 green (itr626-daemon-tests), clippy green (itr626-clippy). Awaiting e2e.

REOPENED 2026-07-19 — acceptance NOT met. Independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of the fix commit dc63cad.

WHAT THE FIX DID ACHIEVE (confirmed by review): producer-side atomicity is correct. ingest_output now fuses parser mutation + seq assignment + output high-water under one lock with broadcast outside it (terminal.rs:183); attach_with fuses boundary/snapshot/subscribe/high-water (terminal.rs:237); input and resize seq assignment take the same lock (terminal.rs:439, :498); catchup_message no longer re-snapshots (terminal.rs:1181). No deadlock or lock-order violation found. The implementer's rebuttal to fix-shape (a) was independently CONFIRMED correct: seq-based dedup alone could not catch a frame whose bytes were in the parser before a seq was assigned.

WHY IT REOPENS (HIGH): the subscribed receiver is left UNDRAINED across the 500 ms persistence wait, the seed query, the catchup build, and its awaited delivery (terminal.rs:237). The forwarder only starts receiving after attach_with returns (server.rs:3253, :3291). The broadcast ring holds 256 frames (terminal.rs:347) of up to 4096 bytes each (terminal.rs:52), so roughly >1 MiB of output arriving during that window makes rx.recv() return Lagged; the server then tells the client to re-attach and terminates the forwarder (server.rs:3312).

So frames with seq >= N — which the new invariant claims are guaranteed delivered because the subscription already existed — can still be EVICTED before the receiver is ever drained. Subscription existing is not the same as delivery being exactly-once. A command emitting several MiB during attach reproduces it. ADR-0012's restated unconditional invariant remains FALSE.

FIX DIRECTION: drain the receiver into a buffer (or start forwarding) concurrently with the seed read/catchup build, rather than leaving it subscribed-but-unread across multiple awaits — or treat Lagged during attach as a retryable condition rather than a terminal one.

TEST GAP (all uncovered): receiver overflow during a pending attach, persistence timeout, a failed-then-successful batch pair, two simultaneous attaches, session end or resize mid-attach. The DUPLICATE test's hook necessarily moved with the fix, and the 200-line mid-stream test is well under the 256-frame ring and passed pre-fix — it is acceptance coverage, not a race reproduction.

issue.title: Seed tail can end mid-ANSI sequence and swallow the authoritative ESC[H ESC[J repaint
issue.context:
Found by an independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of commit e3d29b9, 2026-07-19.

tail_terminal_output trims only at FRAME boundaries (state/terminals.rs:600), but PTY frames are arbitrary ~4096-byte reads, not ANSI boundaries. The newest persisted frame below before_seq may end INSIDE an OSC/DCS/CSI or a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence whose terminator lives in a later, excluded frame.

terminal.rs:990 concatenates the screen snapshot directly after that seed. If the seed leaves xterm's parser inside an OSC/DCS string, the following repaint bytes (ESC[H ESC[J) are consumed as STRING PAYLOAD rather than executed — the screen is never cleared/homed and terminal state is corrupted for that attachment.

The ESC[H ESC[J sequence itself is sound when parsed from a neutral state; the missing invariant is that the seed GUARANTEES neutral parser state before the repaint. Current tests only assert byte presence, never adversarially split input.
issue.acceptance: The seed is guaranteed to leave the client parser in a neutral state before the repaint — either by trimming the seed to a safe boundary, or by emitting a canonical sequence-terminating prefix (e.g. ESC\\ / BEL-safe reset) before the repaint. Backed by a test that deliberately splits an OSC/DCS string and a multi-byte UTF-8 codepoint across the seed boundary and asserts the screen is correctly cleared and rendered.

issue.title: Web client can drop the attach catchup if it arrives before TerminalView registers its handler
issue.context:
Found by an independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review, 2026-07-19.

Terminals.tsx:264 sends TermAttach IMMEDIATELY, but TerminalView does not register its output handler until its effect runs (TerminalView.tsx:91). If the daemon responds before React commits the effect — very plausible over a local Unix socket — useWisphive.ts:323 SILENTLY DISCARDS the catchup. There is no queue, no buffer, and no retry, so the terminal can render blank with no error.

NOTE: this is an independent race from itr#624 and would produce a similar user-visible symptom (empty terminal / nothing to scroll). It is also precisely the failure mode the PO predicted when proposing a readiness callback: the correct fix is a ready signal / buffered delivery, not a timeout.
issue.acceptance: Catchup delivered before a handler registers is buffered and replayed to the handler on registration (or attach is not sent until the consumer is ready), so a fast daemon response can never blank the terminal. Dropping an unroutable message is at minimum logged rather than silent. Covered by a test that delivers catchup before handler registration.

issue.title: TermAttach history denials are silent and unaudited — contradicts ADR-0013's stated auditing guarantee
issue.context:
Found by an independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review, 2026-07-19.

The ACL IS correctly checked before any history is read on every path examined (good). But on the TermAttach path a denial simply returns Vec::new() at server.rs:3245 with NO durable audit row — unlike TermReplay, which audits every request at server.rs:3529.

So the most common way a user hits the boundary (attaching to a session from another device) produces no audit trail at all, and no user-visible explanation. This is part of why the boundary reads as 'the scroll wheel is broken' rather than as a permission decision.

ADR CONTRADICTION: ADR-0012 explicitly documents this silent-denial behavior for attach, while ADR-0013 states denials remain audited and must surface as actionable UI. As shipped, ADR-0013's claim is false. Either ADR-0013 supersedes ADR-0012 on this point (and the code must follow) or ADR-0013 must be corrected. Resolve explicitly rather than leaving a live contradiction in the decision record.
issue.acceptance: A denied or downgraded (screen-only) attach emits a durable audit row equivalent to the TermReplay path, including requester and authorization outcome, and surfaces to the user as actionable UI naming the remedy. The ADR contradiction is resolved in the decision record, with one ADR amended to match the implemented behavior.

issue.title: Attach seed byte cap is not strictly enforced and prefetches up to 512 rows (~2 MiB) before trimming
issue.context:
Found by an independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of commit e3d29b9, 2026-07-19.

state/terminals.rs:606 fetches up to 512 COMPLETE ROWS and only then applies the byte budget. Three consequences:

1. NOT A RELIABLE TAIL: with many small frames, 512 rows can be far LESS than the advertised 256 KiB, so the operator silently gets much less scrollback than ATTACH_SCROLLBACK_SEED_MAX_BYTES implies.
2. NOT A STRICT CAP: the newest frame is deliberately admitted even if it alone exceeds max_bytes (lines 619-625), so an oversized or legacy row breaks the stated bound.
3. MEMORY COST: with normal ~4096-byte PTY frames, SQLite may materialize ~2 MiB per attach before trimming, multiplied across concurrent attaches.

The (session_id, seq) index correctly avoids a table scan on the operator's ~836 MB DB, so this is a materialization/bounding problem rather than a query-plan one. A fixed ROW limit is simply the wrong mechanism for a BYTE limit.
issue.acceptance: The seed is bounded by bytes, not by a fixed row count — the query accumulates backwards until the byte budget is met (or the session start is reached), so the result is a genuine tail of up to the configured size regardless of frame size distribution. The documented cap is a hard maximum, including for a single oversized row. Peak memory per attach is bounded by the byte budget rather than by row-count times frame size.

issue.title: Web auth 401 log line cannot distinguish an unknown token from a revoked one
issue.context:
security_middleware logs a single undifferentiated warning for every device-token rejection:

    crates/wisphive_web/src/security.rs:627
    WARN wisphive_web::security: rejecting request: unknown or revoked device token path="/ws"

lookup_device_token (security.rs:519) collapses three distinct outcomes into Option::None:
  1. no row with that token_hash (token from another wisphive.db, or wiped by reset_web_password)
  2. a row exists but revoked_at IS NOT NULL (find_web_device_by_token_hash, web_auth.rs:277-286, filters `AND revoked_at IS NULL`)
  3. the sqlx query itself errored (security.rs:529-532 warns separately, then returns None)

Case 2 is the common one in practice and is fully self-explanatory server-side, but the operator has to open the DB to see it. Observed 2026-07-19: six devices were bulk-revoked at 09:44:36Z; rejections at 10:11:29Z on /ws then /api/me 123ms later were a stale browser context replaying a token revoked 27 min earlier. Answering "why am I getting 401s" required a sqlite3 -readonly query against web_devices that the log could have answered directly.

PII/secret constraint (non-negotiable): the presented token and its SHA-256 hash MUST NOT be logged in any form, not even truncated. The device *name* is a UA-derived label and should also stay out of the log line. Only the opaque UUIDv4 device id and the revoked_at timestamp are safe to emit.

Implementation sketch: have lookup_device_token return a small enum (Active(row) / Revoked{id, revoked_at} / Unknown) instead of Option, by dropping the `AND revoked_at IS NULL` filter and branching in Rust on revoked_at. The middleware keeps returning the same opaque 401 "invalid device token" to the client — the distinction is server-log-only, so it leaks nothing to an unauthenticated caller.

Related: itr#625 (every login mints a new permanent token — the reason six credentials existed to revoke), itr#364 (revocation does not tear down a live /ws).
issue.acceptance:
A request presenting a token whose web_devices row has revoked_at set logs a distinguishable message including the device UUID and the revoked_at timestamp
A request presenting a token with no matching row logs a distinguishable "unknown" message
Neither log line contains the raw token, any prefix/suffix of it, its SHA-256 hash, or the device name — asserted by a test
The HTTP response for both cases is unchanged: 401 with the same opaque "invalid device token" body (no oracle for an unauthenticated caller)
Covered by unit tests in crates/wisphive_web that exercise both branches

issue.title: Attach persistence-watermark wait: 500ms timeout silently serves an incomplete seed, and runs BEFORE the ACL denial check
issue.context:
Found by independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of dc63cad (the itr#626 fix), 2026-07-19.

The fix added a bounded 500ms wait for the DB batcher's persistence watermark before the seed read, so output still inside the ~50ms batch window is visible to the seed query. Two defects in that new mechanism:

1. SILENT INCOMPLETE SEED ON TIMEOUT. After 500ms, await_output_persisted logs a warning and returns NORMALLY regardless of how far behind the watermark is (terminal.rs:257). The seed read and catchup then proceed (terminal.rs:245) with no error to the client and no audit event. If SQLite is blocked past 500ms and enough below-boundary output has scrolled off the 200-row parser screen, the attach silently serves incomplete scrollback — precisely the silent-gap failure class this mechanism exists to close, just relocated to the timeout path.

2. THE WAIT RUNS BEFORE THE ACL DENIAL CHECK (terminal.rs:245 vs server.rs:3255). A stalled or backed-up batcher therefore taxes EVERY attach 500ms, including attaches that will be denied history anyway. Unauthorized requesters should not be able to make the daemon wait on persistence at all.
issue.acceptance: A persistence wait that times out does not silently degrade: the attach either surfaces the degraded scrollback to the client as visible state, or emits a durable audit/warn event identifying the session and how far behind the watermark was — never a silent partial seed. The wait is performed only AFTER the ACL decision, so a denied requester never pays it and cannot use it as a lever on daemon latency. Covered by a test that forces the timeout path and asserts the degradation is observable.

issue.title: Persistence watermark advances past permanently-dropped rows — it tracks latest-persisted, not contiguous-persisted
issue.context:
Found by independent Codex (gpt-5.6-sol) review of dc63cad, 2026-07-19.

On a batch insert error the batcher warns and UNCONDITIONALLY DISCARDS the failed rows (terminal.rs:1059). A later successful batch then advances the watermark via fetch_max (terminal.rs:1005).

So if rows 1-128 fail and rows 129-256 succeed, the watermark advances past 256 even though 1-128 are permanently absent. The attach seed wait is then satisfied by a watermark that asserts persistence which did not happen, and once those bytes scroll off the parser screen they are gone from scrollback with no gap indicated anywhere.

The value is a 'latest successfully persisted output seq' marker, but it is CONSUMED as if it were a 'contiguous persistence' guarantee. That mismatch is the defect — the seed-completeness reasoning built on it in dc63cad is only as sound as contiguity, which is not maintained.
issue.acceptance: The watermark consumed by the attach seed reflects CONTIGUOUS persistence, or the consumer explicitly accounts for holes. A failed batch is either retried, or recorded such that the watermark cannot advance past the gap and the resulting scrollback discontinuity is surfaced rather than silent. Covered by a test with a failed-then-successful batch pair asserting the watermark does not falsely advance.

issue.title: Terminal forwarder SILENTLY DROPS output frames when conn_tx is full — exactly-once is false on the steady-state path, contradicting ADR-0012
issue.acceptance: Frame loss on a full client channel is either eliminated (backpressure via tx.reserve(), with an in-memory journal absorbing the burst so the PTY reader is never stalled) or made VISIBLE — a typed gap marker on the wire (e.g. TermGap { id, from_seq, to_seq }) that the client renders, plus an audit/warn event. A client must always be able to tell whether its stream is complete. ADR-0012's exactly-once claim is either made true end-to-end or amended to state the conditions under which it holds, and the itr#82 availability decision is explicitly reconciled with it in the decision record.

issue.title: Re-attach aborts the forwarder but leaves its already-queued chunks in conn_tx — stale frames drain AFTER the new catchup
issue.context:
Found by the GPT-5.6-sol council seat, 2026-07-19; verified in code.

The TermAttach arm (server.rs:3211) does:

    if let Some(handle) = term_attachments.remove(&id) { handle.abort(); }

Aborting the task stops it producing NEW frames, but it does NOT purge frames the old forwarder has ALREADY try_send'd into conn_tx (capacity 1024). Those queued TermChunk messages remain in the mpsc buffer and drain to the client AFTER the new catchup is written (server.rs:~3288).

RESULT — cross-generation corruption: bytes from the PREVIOUS attachment generation arrive after the NEW catchup has repainted the screen. The client feeds stale output into a freshly-seeded terminal, so the rendered buffer interleaves two generations. This is independent of broadcast lag and of the itr#626 seam — it survives every fix applied so far.

This is a plausible contributor to confusing terminal state after a refresh/re-attach cycle, and it is invisible to every existing test because none re-attaches while frames are in flight.

PROPOSED FIX (from the same seat): carry an attachment_generation on TermCatchup and TermChunk so the client can discard frames belonging to a superseded generation; alternatively drain/replace the channel on re-attach. Generation tagging is preferable because it also makes the discard observable rather than silent.
issue.acceptance: Frames produced by a superseded attachment can never be rendered after the succeeding attachment's catchup — enforced by an attachment generation (or equivalent) carried on catchup and chunk messages and checked client-side, not by timing. Covered by a test that re-attaches while frames are queued in conn_tx and asserts no pre-abort frame is delivered after the new catchup.

issue.title: Web client ignores frame seq entirely — cannot detect dropped, duplicated, or reordered terminal output
issue.context:
Found by the GPT-5.6-sol council seat, 2026-07-19; verified in code.

The term_chunk handler (useWisphive.ts:~315) decodes msg.data and dispatches it straight to the terminal registration. It never reads a sequence number. A grep for 'seq' across the hook finds only from_seq on the outbound term_replay request (useWisphive.ts:1049) — nothing on the inbound path.

CONSEQUENCE: the client has NO way to detect a gap, a duplicate, or a reordering in its own output stream. It renders whatever arrives, in arrival order, and reports nothing. This is why every delivery defect in this area (itr#626, itr#634, the cross-generation stale-chunk bug) presents to the user as inexplicable terminal weirdness rather than as a detectable fault — and why they were all found by code review rather than by the running system.

This matters more once the daemon-side work lands: emitting gap markers or generation tags is pointless if the client cannot act on sequence information. Client-side validation is the half that makes daemon-side guarantees observable.
issue.acceptance: The web client tracks the expected next sequence per attached terminal and detects discontinuities. A gap, duplicate, or reordering is surfaced — at minimum a console/telemetry signal and a visible in-terminal discontinuity marker rather than silent mis-rendering — and duplicates are discarded rather than double-rendered. The TUI client is assessed for the same gap.

issue.title: Track the issue tracker as a diffable JSONL snapshot (.itr/issues.jsonl) with a freshness check
issue.context: The tracker (.itr.db, SQLite) is gitignored, so a fresh clone has no issues although ~2,000 itr#NNN references live in tracked docs/commits. itr v3.3.1 export is byte-deterministic, id-sorted JSONL and import into a fresh DB is now content-lossless (issue ids preserved; notes/events/relations get fresh surrogate row ids). Track the export as .itr/issues.jsonl, regenerate it via a just recipe, and guard it with a normalizing freshness check wired into docs-lint. Same pattern as the e2e evidence split (a1223ce): live output stays gitignored, the reviewed snapshot is tracked.
issue.acceptance: 1. just itr-snapshot writes .itr/issues.jsonl atomically from itr export (never truncates on a failed export). 2. just itr-snapshot-check (and just docs-lint) exits 1 with the changed/added/removed issue ids when the snapshot is stale, 0 when fresh, and passes on a clone restored via just itr-restore despite renumbered note/event/relation ids. 3. just itr-restore rebuilds .itr.db from the snapshot on a fresh clone with identical issue ids and content (verified by re-export compare). 4. CONTRIBUTING.md + CLAUDE.md document restore/snapshot/single-writer rules.
